data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"A decentralized network of small services is more resilient to correlated failure than a single large service because it replaces 'homogeneous redundancy' with 'heterogeneous diversity', shifting the failure boundary from a single point of systemic collapse to a fragmented landscape of partial outages.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The decentralized network converges on a 'standard' stack for cost efficiency (the 'Diversity Debt' described in SCR_003), erasing the heterogeneity advantage.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The failure is triggered by a universal protocol-level vulnerability (e.g., a flaw in the shared API specification) rather than an implementation-level bug.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The coordination overhead of the decentralized network introduces a new, centralized point of failure in the discovery or routing layer.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The large service relies on internal redundancy (replication), which creates a high-density target for 'common-mode failures' (e.g., a single bug in the consensus logic or a shared kernel version). In contrast, decentralized services typically utilize diverse hardware, OS versions, and implementation stacks. This 'Architectural Distance' (as hinted in SCR_007) ensures that a trigger causing a crash in one node is unlikely to be present in another, thereby converting a potential total system failure into a series of uncorrelated, localized events.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
